recent_posts.title: Fresh 2.3: Zero JS by default, View Transitions, and Temporal support
recent_posts.summary: Fresh 2.3 delivers on its zero-JavaScript-by-default promise by only injecting client scripts when islands or partials are actually used, dropping 14–22 KB from static pages. New features include View Transitions API integration via a single HTML attribute, first-class WebSocket support with managed and bare modes, CSP nonce injection, IP filter middleware with CIDR support, OpenTelemetry server-to-browser trace propagation, Temporal API support in island props, multiple static directories, loading indicators on form submissions, and reverse proxy support. The release also includes significant Vite integration improvements, dropping two Babel passes, and numerous routing and partials bug fixes.

recent_posts.title: Deno 2.7
recent_posts.summary: Deno 2.7 ships several notable improvements: full support for the Temporal API as a modern replacement for the legacy Date object, native Windows on ARM builds eliminating x86 emulation overhead, and support for the package.json overrides field for better Node.js compatibility. The release also introduces a simplified subprocess API, a new `deno create` command for project scaffolding, a `--compile` flag for installing npm packages as standalone executables, a `--self-extracting` flag for compiled binaries to extract embedded files to disk, and a `--check-js` flag for type-checking JavaScript files from the CLI.

recent_posts.title: Deno Subhosting — Roll out changes across all your customers with Layers.
recent_posts.summary: Deno Subhosting's Layers feature lets platform operators apply configuration changes across thousands of hosted applications simultaneously without redeploying each one. A demo using the new Python SDK (deno-sandbox) shows creating a shared layer with an environment variable, attaching it to multiple apps, and updating the variable once to instantly propagate the change to all apps. Future support for shared code files across applications is also planned.

recent_posts.title: OpenTelemetry support in Deno Subhosting — observability at scale
recent_posts.summary: Deno Subhosting allows platforms to programmatically deploy and run untrusted user code at scale. A key challenge is observability across potentially hundreds of thousands of deployed apps. Deno Deploy addresses this with built-in OpenTelemetry support, automatically instrumenting console.log calls, incoming HTTP requests, and outbound fetches as traces and spans. Developers can also add custom OTel instrumentation using the standard @opentelemetry/api. To integrate with existing observability stacks, Deno Deploy supports an OTLP firehose — a configurable endpoint that streams all telemetry data to external platforms. A live demo shows configuring Honeycomb as the destination by setting the endpoint URL and an API key header in the Deno Deploy dashboard, after which traces and logs appear automatically in Honeycomb.

recent_posts.title: Deno Deploy now supports serverless Postgres with automatic multi-environment provisioning
recent_posts.summary: Deno Deploy now supports provisioning serverless PostgreSQL databases directly within the platform, not just connecting to external ones. It automatically provisions separate databases for production, preview, and local development environments. A pre-deploy command allows running migrations automatically at the end of the build process, before deployment, eliminating the need to manually run migrations for each database context.

recent_posts.title: Snapshot your Deno Sandbox setup for speedy start-up
recent_posts.summary: Deno Sandbox supports volume snapshots that dramatically reduce cloud sandbox boot times to under 200 milliseconds. Instead of reinstalling packages on every boot, you set up a volume once, install your dependencies (e.g., Python, NumPy), snapshot the disk with `client.volumes.snapshot`, and then reuse that snapshot as the root volume when creating new sandboxes via `client.sandbox.create`. This approach is especially useful for per-request or per-user sandbox provisioning where cold-start latency is a dealbreaker.

recent_posts.title: Safe Cloud Code Execution with Snapshots (Python Pre-Installed, Zero Wait)
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough showing how to run untrusted Python code safely in isolated cloud sandboxes using the Deno Sandbox SDK. The approach uses a two-step snapshot pattern: first, a setup script installs Python, pip, numpy, pandas, and other packages into a cloud volume, then snapshots it. Subsequent runs boot from that snapshot in under 200ms with no reinstallation needed. A Mandelbrot fractal explorer served as a live web app demonstrates the technique. The pattern is applicable to AI-generated code execution, user-uploaded scripts, and multi-tenant data analysis tools where isolation and reproducibility are critical.

recent_posts.title: Create a coding sandbox from your browser. #coding #programming
Build a dinosaur runner game with Deno, pt. 6
recent_posts.summary: The sixth and final part of a Deno dinosaur runner game tutorial series focuses on adding observability to a production-ready web application. It covers setting up structured JSON logging via middleware, implementing custom OpenTelemetry traces with spans and attributes for key routes (score submission, leaderboard fetch, customization), and leveraging Deno Deploy's built-in Logs, Traces, and Metrics dashboards. The post explains how to correlate logs with traces, use span attributes for filtering, and interpret platform metrics like HTTP latency, CPU usage, and GC time. It also demonstrates using Deno Deploy's tunnel feature to verify instrumentation locally before deploying.

recent_posts.title: Deno Sandbox — instant Linux microVMs  #coding #ai
recent_posts.summary: Deno Deploy now supports instant Linux microVMs via a new `deno sandbox` subcommand. Running `deno sandbox create --sh` provisions a cloud-hosted Linux VM and SSH-connects to it in under a second. Sandboxes are ephemeral — they disappear when the SSH session ends. The feature also includes a secrets mechanism that never exposes raw secret values to sandbox code; secrets are only injected at the network level when outbound requests are made to specified hosts.
